content:
Global maritime trade — the system that carries more than 80 per cent of everything the world buys and sells — is set to record zero growth in 2026, the United Nations trade and development agency said on Thursday, as four critical shipping chokepoints come under pressure at the same time.

The warning comes in UN Trade and Development's (UNCTAD) flagship Review of Maritime Transport 2026, published in Geneva on 26 November. Seaborne trade volumes reached 12.3 billion tonnes in 2025, but growth slowed to 1.9 per cent — half the 3.9 per cent pace of 2024. For this year the agency projects no growth at all, followed by a recovery of 3.2 per cent in 2027, according to [UN News](https://news.un.org/en/story/2026/11/1168884).

The headline figure hides a paradox that runs through the whole report: ships are sailing further even as the amount of cargo stays flat. Demand measured in ton-miles — the volume of goods multiplied by the distance travelled — is projected to rise by 1.5 per cent in 2026, because disruptions are forcing vessels onto longer routes. Container trade is forecast to grow 3.3 per cent, a slower pace than in 2025.

Four waterways sit at the centre of the problem. The Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea and Suez Canal corridor, the Black Sea and the Panama Canal are all under strain simultaneously, and each one is, in the words of UNCTAD Acting Secretary-General Pedro Manuel Moreno, among the hardest routes in the world to replace. They offer the shortest and most efficient routes between two seas, "and in some cases, the only route," he said at the report's launch.

The sharpest shock came in the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow passage that carries roughly a fifth of the world's oil supply as well as major fertiliser exports. Before the disruption, around 120 ships crossed the strait every day. After the escalation of the conflict in the Middle East in late February 2026, traffic measured by gross tonnage had fallen by roughly 95 per cent by early March, UNCTAD said. Attacks on shipping linked to the Iran-US war created what Moreno described as a near-standstill in the flow of oil and gas through the waterway, and the disruption has continued to shape the region's shipping since — the United States has destroyed Iranian oil tankers at sea this year, and Tehran has retaliated, as reported in [Global Wire's coverage of the tanker war](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/us-destroys-five-iranian-tankers-iran-retaliates-jordan-november-2026).

Insurance costs captured the panic in days. War risk premiums for a 100 million dollar tanker reportedly jumped from about 200,000 dollars to 1 million dollars per voyage within days of the disruption in Hormuz, according to UNCTAD. Container lines added emergency war risk charges and fuel surcharges to cover their higher operating costs, and container spot rates more than doubled between January and August 2026.

In the Red Sea, insecurity since late 2023 has pushed many ships to abandon the Suez Canal route and sail around the Cape of Good Hope instead, adding roughly 30 per cent to average voyage distances on Asia-Europe container routes. Some shipping companies have resumed operations through the Red Sea, but many vessels continue to use the longer route. The fighting around the Red Sea's southern approaches has also continued: coalition forces struck the Yemeni port of Hodeidah this month after the Houthis threatened Saudi ports, as [Global Wire reported](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/ar/articles/coalition-strikes-hodeidah-port-houthis-threaten-saudi-ports-november-2026). Meanwhile, grain shipments through the Black Sea remain exposed to security risks, and changing traffic patterns and restrictions have affected operations in the Panama Canal.

For ordinary people, the report's message is blunt. "When shipping costs rise, consumers ultimately pay the price: but not everybody pays it equally," Moreno said. Economies with little capacity to absorb shocks have suffered most from costlier fuel and greater transport and production costs, which have pushed up food prices and inflation. "Small island economies and least developed countries are particularly exposed," he stressed, because the imports they rely on often require multiple shipping connections. "Every additional mile means more fuel, more time, and more cost."

If the current fuel shock continues into 2027, higher shipping costs alone could push consumer price rises in the least developed countries to almost twice the global average, the report warns. "Disruption in one critical maritime corridor can quickly become a cost-of-living crisis thousands of miles away," Moreno explained. "This is how disruptions to maritime transport translate into higher costs of living and widen inequalities between economies."

The report does find one brighter trend. So-called South-South container routes, linking markets, manufacturing centres and ports across Asia, Africa, the Middle East and Latin America, grew by 12.1 per cent last year and accounted for nearly a third of the growth in containerised trade. And over the past two decades, least developed countries — most of them in Africa — have improved their shipping connectivity three times faster than the rest of the world. "These gains matter, but they do not remove the underlying vulnerabilities," Moreno cautioned.

UNCTAD's answer is a shift from reacting to each crisis to preparing for the next one. The Review of Maritime Transport 2026 urges shared stocks of food staples and fuel, along with pre-agreed alternative trade routes and customs procedures to keep essential goods moving when a corridor closes. It also flags a growing concern over potential overcapacity in container shipping, where heavy newbuilding deliveries, limited recycling and a possible normalisation of Red Sea traffic could upset the balance between supply and demand.

For now, the agency's verdict is that trade kept moving in 2026 despite the disruptions — but on longer, costlier voyages, with the bill landing hardest on the countries least able to pay it.
summary: UN Trade and Development projects zero growth in global seaborne trade in 2026 as the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea, the Black Sea and the Panama Canal come under pressure at the same time, warning that the poorest countries will pay the highest price.
title: Global maritime trade set for zero growth in 2026 as four chokepoints come under pressure at once, UN warns
